analysis.one_liner: Strengthens the federal ethics office's power to investigate and punish executive branch conflicts of interest.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2019 with six Democratic sponsors, referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give the Office of Government Ethics — the small agency that oversees ethics rules for the executive branch — real enforcement teeth. It could subpoena documents and witnesses, order corrective action like divesting conflicting holdings, and impose penalties such as suspension, demotion, or dismissal on officials who violate ethics rules. It would also make the office the central public repository for financial disclosure reports, recusals, waivers, and ethics records, and it would extend ethics oversight to White House and Executive Office of the President staff, including unpaid advisers. The ethics director could only be removed for cause, protecting the job from political retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens get a watchdog with real power instead of one that can only issue advisory opinions: an independent office that can compel evidence, force divestitures, punish officials who ignore ethics rulings, and post conflict-of-interest records where anyone can read them. Career federal employees and whistleblowers also benefit from rules applied evenly up to the White House staff level.

how_it_helps.text: The Office of Government Ethics could issue subpoenas for documents and witness testimony during investigations, enforced through federal court if refused.
The office could order corrective actions such as divestiture and impose administrative remedies including reprimand, suspension, demotion, or dismissal on officials who violate ethics rules.

The office would become the central repository of all conflict-of-interest laws, recusals, waivers, and exemptions, and would post financial disclosure reports and public ethics records online in a searchable, downloadable format at no charge.
Ethics oversight would explicitly cover White House and Executive Office of the President staff, including unpaid advisers, closing a gap in current law.
The ethics director could be removed only for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance, insulating the office from political pressure.

analysis.who_pays: Executive branch officials and White House staff who would face investigation, forced divestiture, or discipline for ethics violations, plus agencies bearing the administrative cost of new training, registration, and reporting requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves the President out of direct enforcement: the ethics office may only 'recommend' corrective action with respect to the President, so the most powerful official would face the weakest sanction.

Giving a single unelected office subpoena power and final authority over discipline across the executive branch raises fair-process and separation-of-powers concerns that critics of an expanded ethics enforcer would press, particularly when applied to the White House.
The mandate for training, registration, and reporting by every agency ethics official adds administrative burden and cost across the executive branch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is favorable: enforcement teeth and public records for an ethics office that currently cannot compel evidence or punish violators, at a modest administrative cost. The design is not perfect — the President himself is beyond the office's reach, and consolidating subpoena and disciplinary power in one unelected director invites abuse arguments — but on balance the public gains more oversight than it gives up.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee from the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on March 27, 2019, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Senators Hirono, Klobuchar, Udall, Whitehouse, and Duckworth.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executive branch officials and White House staff are better off: they remain under an ethics office that can advise and recommend but cannot compel evidence, order divestiture, or impose discipline, and no independent public repository of their recusals and waivers exists.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand the Office of Government Ethics' investigative and disciplinary powers.

for.name: Sens. Hirono, Klobuchar, Udall, Whitehouse, and Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators signed on.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it during the entire Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority controlling the Senate floor and calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it had no path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats; not a single Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run committee and Senate took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Executive branch officials and White House staff
industries.note: The bill would expose these officials to subpoenas, forced divestiture, and discipline, and would publish their recusals and waivers. Their interest in avoiding enforcement runs directly against the public's interest in transparency, and they are the group best served by the bill's death.
The ethics office would gain subpoena power, disciplinary authority, and control over all executive branch ethics records — powers it currently lacks. Its gain is the public's gain in this design.
